update_policy: Manually reviewed snapshot. Review quarterly or when a source publishes a new edition; values do not update automatically.

metrics.title: Electricity generated
metrics.interpretation: More electricity was generated. The total alone does not establish cleaner energy, universal access, or dependable delivery.
metrics.definition: World electricity_generation series in the OWID energy dataset; annual electrical output, not primary energy or installed nameplate capacity.
metrics.limitation: Generation includes energy later lost or used within the energy system. It is not a measure of useful work delivered to homes and businesses, and must not be substituted into the primary-energy baseline above.
metrics.source_name: Our World in Data, Energy dataset
metrics.next_step: Pair new output with emissions, curtailment and reliability measures.

metrics.title: People without electricity
metrics.interpretation: The access gap remains large. The 2026 report describes a plateau in the global access rate, despite gains in some regions.
metrics.definition: People lacking basic electricity access, as reported in Tracking SDG 7: The Energy Progress Report 2026, for 2024.
metrics.limitation: A connection does not establish reliable service or affordability. No numeric year-over-year change is inferred by subtracting totals from different report editions, which may revise history.
metrics.source_name: World Bank and SDG 7 partner agencies, 2026 report
metrics.source_evidence: The 2026 release reports 655 million without electricity and describes the 2024 global access rate as stagnant at 92%.
metrics.next_step: Track affordable, reliable connections, especially in underserved regions.

metrics.title: Energy-related CO₂
metrics.interpretation: Emissions grew more slowly, but still reached a new high. Slower growth is not an absolute reduction.
metrics.definition: IEA's headline global energy-related CO₂ total, including fuel combustion, industrial processes and fugitive flaring.
metrics.limitation: Not all greenhouse gases or all human-caused emissions. The growth rate comes from the same 2026 report; it is not calculated against the older 2025 report's unrevised total.
metrics.source_evidence: The report gives nearly 38.4 Gt in 2025, about 145 Mt higher than 2024, and growth around 0.4%.
metrics.next_step: Measure absolute emissions alongside low-emission generation.

metrics.title: Time to grid connection
metrics.change_label: Increasing duration, reported by Berkeley Lab
metrics.interpretation: Projects that reach operation face long waits. A shrinking queue alone is not proof that connection has become faster.
metrics.definition: Median time from interconnection request to commercial operation for projects built in 2025, in regions with available data in Queued Up 2026.
metrics.limitation: A US completed-project cohort, not a global average or the expected wait for a new application. Withdrawn and still-active projects are not in this completion-time median; no exact year-over-year delta is claimed.
metrics.source_name: Berkeley Lab and GridTracker, Queued Up 2026
metrics.source_evidence: The 2026 summary says the time to commercial operations is increasing and the median exceeded five years for projects built in 2025 where data are available.
metrics.next_step: Separate study, equipment, permitting and construction delays.

metrics.title: Time without power
metrics.change_label: Nearly 2× the prior decade's annual average
metrics.interpretation: Major events accounted for 80% of interruption hours in 2024. Resilience to extreme weather matters alongside routine service reliability.
metrics.definition: EIA's average non-momentary interruption duration per US electricity customer, including major events, from Electric Power Annual 2024.
metrics.limitation: Compared with the 2014–2023 average, not just 2023. Major events dominate variation; this is not a weather-normalized trend or a worldwide reliability score.
metrics.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Annual 2024 / December 2025 analysis
metrics.source_evidence: EIA reports an average of 11 hours in 2024, nearly twice the preceding decade's annual average; major events account for 80%.
metrics.next_step: Publish both all-event and normal-weather reliability measures.

metrics.title: Residential electricity price
metrics.interpretation: The nominal unit price increased. This is a price indicator, not a direct measure of household energy affordability.
metrics.definition: EIA's US residential annual average retail electricity price: 17.30 cents/kWh in the preliminary 2025 series, versus 16.48 in the 2024 annual table.
metrics.limitation: 2025 is preliminary and may be revised. Not inflation-adjusted; bills also depend on usage, and affordability depends on income and other costs. This is not a global energy-burden measure.
metrics.source_name: EIA, Energy Explained and Electric Power Annual table 2.4
metrics.source_evidence: Energy Explained cites 2025 residential 17.30 cents/kWh from February 2026 preliminary data; annual table 2.4 reports 16.48 for 2024.
metrics.next_step: Add household energy burden and inflation-adjusted prices before judging affordability.
